turns.learner: Hello teacher! I want to practise talking about time and life, maybe how long I did things. I am not sure I am good at it.
turns.tutor:
Hello! Good plan, and don't worry. We will practise step by step.

First, a quick question. When you talk about something that happened and is finished, like a trip last year, which verb form do you use?

Now try this: write one sentence about a place you lived, or a job or school you had. Say how long it was, for example "for three years". Then I will help you look at it.

turns.learner: I use past simple I think. I lived in Cairo for twenty years. I still live there now. Is it correct?
turns.tutor:
Thank you for a clear sentence. Using "for twenty years" is a good way to say how long.

Past simple is right for finished things, like your trip last year. Your sentence has two parts, though: "I lived in Cairo for twenty years" and "I still live there now."

Look at "now". Does your life in Cairo belong to the past only, or does it continue?

Tell me why you chose "lived" for this sentence. What made you pick it?

turns.learner: I chose lived because twenty years is a time in the past, I think. The life continues but the twenty years already happened?
turns.tutor:
Thank you for explaining your idea. You are right that twenty years of your life have already happened.

But past simple is for a time that is finished. It does not work well when the time reaches now.

Compare two people:
A: lives in Cairo now, since twenty years ago.
B: lived in Cairo for twenty years, then moved to Alexandria.

Which person has a finished time in Cairo, A or B? Tell me how you decided.

turns.learner: B is finished, because B moved to Alexandria. A is still there. So for A maybe I live in Cairo for twenty years? I am not sure.
turns.tutor:
Well done. You are right: B has a finished time in Cairo, because B moved. And A is still there. That is clear thinking, even if you feel unsure.

Now look at your sentence for A: "I live in Cairo for twenty years."

Check the verb part only. "live" talks about now. But your sentence also needs to show twenty years of time before now.

Can you change the verb part so it shows both? Try again.

turns.learner: Maybe I have lived in Cairo for twenty years? I think I saw this form before, but I am not confident.
turns.tutor:
Yes, "I have lived in Cairo for twenty years" is correct. It shows a time that started in the past and continues now. You can trust your memory here.

Now try this exercise:

Complete: "She ___ (have) this car since March." Write the verb phrase.

Tell me the rule in your own words.

turns.learner: She has had this car since March. Rule: if it still continues now, I use have plus past part, not past simple. Maybe?
turns.tutor:
Yes, "She has had this car since March" is correct, and your rule is right. You can be more confident.

Quick recap:
Remember: "if it still continues now", use "have" plus the past part, as in "I have lived in Cairo for twenty years".
If the time is finished, like when B moved to Alexandria, past simple is the right choice.

Tell me the rule in your own words.
